task_comparisons.frozen_first_answer: Both pathways begin when the hypothalamus releases GnRH, which stimulates the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH. In the testis, FSH acts on Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules to support developing sperm. LH acts on interstitial or Leydig cells to stimulate testosterone production; testosterone helps support sperm development. Testosterone also inhibits upstream stimulation, while Sertoli-cell inhibin particularly restrains FSH. In the ovary, FSH supports follicular development and LH also contributes to ovarian hormone production. A growing follicle releases estrogen. Sustained high estrogen before ovulation switches to a temporary positive-feedback effect, producing a sharp pituitary LH surge. That surge helps release the secondary oocyte and form the corpus luteum from the remaining follicular tissue. The comparison is therefore a shared GnRH-pituitary start with different gonadal targets and outcomes: Sertoli/Leydig support of sperm development versus follicular development and an LH-triggered ovulation sequence.
task_comparisons.original_model: Both begin with hypothalamic GnRH and anterior-pituitary FSH/LH. In males FSH supports Sertoli cells and LH stimulates interstitial-cell testosterone production. In females FSH supports follicular development, estrogen rises, and sustained high estrogen promotes an LH surge that triggers ovulation and corpus-luteum formation. Feedback differs with the stage of the cycle.

task_comparisons.frozen_first_answer: The LH surge and ovulation have already occurred in this case. If the corpus luteum does not remain active, its progesterone and estrogen output will fall. With less progesterone, the endometrium loses its normal luteal support, so the functional lining is likely to break down and be shed rather than remain maintained. This is a hormone-production/support failure after ovulation; it does not undo the earlier release of the oocyte. An oviduct blockage is instead a transport problem: it can stop or reduce gamete encounter or onward movement toward the uterus even while ovarian hormones and cycles continue. A blockage does not by itself demonstrate inactive corpus-luteum tissue.
task_comparisons.original_model: Reduced corpus-luteum activity means reduced progesterone and estrogen support for the endometrium. The lining may not be maintained. An oviduct blockage instead disrupts transport and may occur even with normal ovarian hormone activity. Neither description alone provides a complete personal diagnosis.

task_comparisons.frozen_first_answer: A normal progesterone concentration means that the hormone is available to the tissue; it does not show that the target can use it. Endometrial cells need functioning progesterone receptors to recognize the signal and produce their normal response. Here those receptors do not function, so normal hormone availability need not give normal maintenance of the lining. The stated problem is at the target-cell response step, not evidence that the corpus luteum has failed to produce progesterone. The tissue model also does not itself measure where the supplied progesterone was produced. Increasing supply alone would not establish a restored receptor response.
task_comparisons.original_model: A normal progesterone concentration is evidence about hormone availability, not receptor function. Endometrial cells need functioning receptors for the usual progesterone response. The model can have normal ovarian hormone production but reduced support of the lining because the target cannot respond normally.

task_comparisons.frozen_first_answer: In the original A/B comparison, both tissues receive the same estrogen concentration, but only B receives the added chemical and B has a weaker response. The separate binding test says the chemical occupies estrogen receptors without activating them. It may therefore reduce estrogen’s opportunity to activate those receptors, weakening the response even when estrogen supply is unchanged. I would keep exposure duration the same in A and B: a shorter exposure could otherwise explain a weaker response. These observations cannot establish a safe exposure level for people. Tissue samples do not show whole-body absorption, distribution or breakdown, and this case gives no real exposure amounts or population outcomes. The evidence supports this receptor-interference model under the stated conditions; it does not prove that receptor interference is the only cellular contribution. The C/D example concerns a different activating chemical and does not change the original A/B non-activating result.
task_comparisons.original_model: The added chemical occupies receptors without activating them, potentially reducing estrogen signalling. Estrogen concentration, tissue type and exposure conditions should be comparable. A tissue result does not establish a safe dose or predict every effect in a whole organism.
